questions.q: What does Salesforce's 'Identity Location' SAML setting control?
options: Which physical data center processes the login request
Where in the SAML assertion Salesforce looks for the identity value -- either the Subject (NameID) or an Attribute element
Which Salesforce profile a new user is assigned on creation
The IP address range allowed to submit SAML assertions
questions.explain: Identity Location tells Salesforce whether to read the mapped identity value from the Subject/NameID or from an Attribute element -- getting this setting wrong is a common real-world SSO misconfiguration.

questions.q: What does the SAML assertion's Signature element prove?
options: That the user has administrator permissions
That the assertion wasn't altered in transit and actually came from the IdP it claims to be from, validated against the IdP's configured public certificate
That the user's session will never time out
That Just-in-Time provisioning is enabled
questions.explain: The signature is a cryptographic proof of authenticity and integrity, checked against the IdP's certificate configured in Salesforce's SAML SSO setup.

questions.q: Why does supporting multiple Identity Providers in one Salesforce org require more than just adding a second SAML SSO configuration?
options: Because Salesforce only allows one SAML configuration per org, making this scenario impossible
Because Salesforce also needs a way to determine which SAML configuration applies to a given login attempt, typically resolved by routing users to different login endpoints per IdP
Because a second IdP requires disabling Just-in-Time provisioning entirely
Because multiple IdPs can only be supported using OAuth, never SAML
questions.explain: With multiple SAML configurations active, Salesforce needs a deliberate routing mechanism to know which configuration a given login attempt should be validated against, rather than inferring it after the fact.

questions.q: Per this lesson, which federation mechanism is more typically used for customer- or partner-facing external login, as opposed to workforce SSO?
options: SAML is used exclusively for all federation scenarios, including customer logins
OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect (OIDC)-based external login, more commonly used for customer- or partner-facing identity than SAML, which more commonly fits workforce SSO
Federation ID mapping replaces the need for any federation protocol in customer-facing scenarios
Just-in-Time provisioning is itself a separate federation protocol from both SAML and OAuth
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes the two: SAML is the typical fit for Doverfield's employee SSO, while OAuth/OIDC is more typically used when customers or partners log in with an existing external identity.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say session security policy is a separate decision from SAML authentication itself?
options: Because successfully authenticating a user answers 'who is this,' not 'how long should their session last, from what network, on what device' -- those are configured independently
Because session security policies are only available for OAuth, never SAML
Because session timeout is automatically set to match the SAML assertion's expiration
Because Salesforce does not support any session security policies at all
questions.explain: Authentication and session governance answer different questions -- a federation design review that only covers authentication leaves session policy (timeout, IP restriction, high-assurance requirements) separately undecided.
